newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea ruling party peace gesture on strike eve.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea ruling party peace gesture on strike eve.

text.p: The chairman of South Korea's ruling party made a dramatic visit on Monday to a Seoul cathedral where union leaders are sheltering from arrest as they plot the biggest strike in the nation's history.
Plans for all-out stoppages starting on Tuesday appeared to be wavering, with hardened union activists confessing workers were losing their appetite for confrontation.
But a brief standoff at Myongdong Cathedral between riot police and 1,500 protesters led by priests and nuns showed feeling was still running high over a controversial labour law.
Witnesses said police blocked the protesters as they tried to march out of the cathedral grounds into a central Seoul shopping district.

They said scores of grim-faced priests pressed against police shields in a standoff that lasted 20 minutes before the marchers turned back. It was the first time clergy members as a group had joined street protests against the new legislation.
Unions have threatened the biggest ever strike on Tuesday and Wednesday over the law, which gives employers the right to lay off workers and replace strikers.
The defence ministry said military personnel were ready to step in to keep essential services running.
Continuing a charm offensive that has stolen the thunder from militant union leaders holed up at the cathedral, New Korea Party leader Lee Hong-koo sought a meeting with activists.
Lee was shoved aside by workers chanting "Get Out" and met instead with South Korea's Roman Catholic Cardinal.
He has challenged heads of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to a televised debate over the law.
Confederation leaders said they would only meet Lee if the government scrapped the law that has sparked three weeks of industrial unrest and dropped arrest warrants against them.
President Kim Young-sam made clear the law would not be scrapped or amended.

"The stark reality facing us today is that without the labour reforms, workers will get neither the income nor jobs in the face of cut-throat global economic competition," he told ruling party lawmakers.
Tuesday's strikes are being spearheaded by the officially recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions. It has called for a two-day walkout by its 1.2 million members.
However, by late on Monday there were signs that stoppages may have only a token impact.
Bank unions said as many as half of all tellers would show up as usual. Subway unions said drivers would confine their protests to wearing street clothes instead of uniforms.
Stock investors were unruffled and the market finished flat, with some blue-chips even posting slight gains.
Union leaders in Ulsan, home of the giant Hyundai Group and traditional hotbed of worker militancy, admitted that sentiment was turning against industrial action.
Lee's headline-grabbing visit to Myongdong Cathedral appeared designed to soften the government's image. Threats to arrest union leaders have recalled the harsh methods of past authoritarian regimes.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung warned confederation leaders they could not evade the law forever.
Yonhap news agency quoted him as saying police would hold back from making arrests "out of respect for freedom of religion and the church's dignity", but eventually there would be a reckoning.
Official figures showed production losses from strikes since the labour bill was rammed through parliament on December 26 had hit 1.96 trillion won ($2.3 billion).
